t.5.37.1: Then, having given the jewel, Sītā spoke to Hanūmān: "This token is truly well known to Rāma."
t.5.37.2: Seeing the jewel, the heroic Rāma will surely remember three: his mother, me, and King Daśaratha.
t.5.37.3: So you, O best of monkeys, urged on once more to vigorous effort, consider carefully what must be done next in this undertaking of the task.
t.5.37.4: You are the authority in carrying out this task, O best of monkeys. Consider what effort toward it would bring about the end of sorrow.
t.5.37.5: Promising "So be it," Māruti of fearsome valor bowed his head to Vaidehī and set about departing.
t.5.37.6: Knowing that the monkey, the son of Māruta, had set out to depart, the queen Maithilī spoke these words in a voice choked with tears.
t.5.37.8: You should arrange matters so that the mighty-armed Rāghava rescues me from this confinement in a sea of sorrow.
t.5.37.9: O Hanumān, you must speak in such a way that the glorious Rāma may find me still alive; by your words, attain merit.
t.5.37.7: O Hanumān, you should convey my wishes for their well-being to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa together, to Sugrīva along with his ministers, and to all the elder monkeys.
t.5.37.11: As soon as he hears from you the words bearing my message, the heroic Rāghava will duly arrange the plan of valorous action.
t.5.37.10: And on hearing the words spoken by me, ever filled with zeal, the valour of Dāśarathi will grow for the sake of winning me back.
t.5.37.12: Having heard those words of Sītā, Hanumān, the son of Māruta, placed his joined palms upon his head and spoke these words in reply.
t.5.37.13: Soon Kākutstha will come, surrounded by the foremost of the monkeys and bears, he who, having conquered his enemies in battle, will dispel your sorrow.
t.5.37.14: For I see no one among mortals, nor among the gods or the asuras, who could dare to stand before him as he spews forth his arrows.
t.5.37.15: For he is able to withstand in battle even the Sun, even Parjanya, even Yama, the son of Vivasvat, and all the more so for your sake.
t.5.37.16: For he desires to rule the earth bounded by the ocean, and Rāma's victory, O daughter of Janaka, rests upon you.
t.5.37.17: Having heard his words, which were fitting, true and well spoken, Jānakī esteemed them highly, and then she spoke these words.
t.5.37.18: Then Sītā, gazing again and again at him as he set out, out of friendship honored him with words filled with love for her husband.
t.5.37.19: Or, if you think it fit, O hero, O subduer of foes, stay for a single day in some hidden place, and having rested, you will depart tomorrow.
t.5.37.20: If only, O valiant one, through your nearness there might be for me, so ill-fated, release from this great sorrow even for a moment!
t.5.37.22: O monkey, the grief born of no longer seeing you would torment me all the more, as if setting me ablaze, I who am already struck by sorrow upon sorrow.
t.5.37.21: For once you have gone, O tiger among monkeys, then until your return even my life would be in doubt; of this there is no doubt.
t.5.37.23: And this very great doubt, O hero, stands as it were before me, O lord of monkeys, concerning your companions, the monkeys and bears.
t.5.37.24: How indeed will those armies of monkeys and bears, or those two sons of the best of men, cross the great ocean that is so hard to cross?
t.5.37.25: Only three beings could have the power to leap across the ocean here: Vainateya, you, or Māruta.
t.5.37.26: Therefore, O hero, in this undertaking of the task, so hard to accomplish, what solution do you see? For you are the foremost of those who know how tasks are done.
t.5.37.28: If, with his entire forces, he were to conquer Rāvaṇa in battle and, victorious, return with me to his own city, that indeed would bring glory to me.
t.5.37.29: But if Kākutstha, the crusher of enemy armies, were to fill Laṅkā with his forces and then lead me away, that would be worthy of him.
t.5.37.30: So bring it about in such a way that his valorous deed may be worthy of that great-souled one, the hero in battle.
t.5.37.27: Indeed, you alone are fully capable of accomplishing this task, O slayer of enemy heroes; this rising of your strength brings you glory.
t.5.37.31: Having heard that speech, rich in meaning, well-composed and supported by reasons, Hanumān spoke the remaining words in reply.
t.5.37.32: O queen, Sugrīva, lord of the armies of monkeys and bears and foremost among the leapers, endowed with great strength, has firmly resolved to act on your behalf.
t.5.37.33: Surrounded by crores of thousands of monkeys, he, the destroyer of the rākṣasas, will swiftly come here, O Vaidehī.
t.5.37.34: Under his command stand monkeys endowed with valour, full of courage and of mighty strength, who rush wherever they will as swift as thought.
t.5.37.35: Those whose movement is not obstructed above, nor below, nor sideways, and who, being of boundless energy, do not falter in great undertakings.
t.5.37.36: Again and again the earth, with its oceans and mountains, has been circled by those greatly energetic ones, following the path of the wind.
t.5.37.37: There, in Sugrīva's presence, are forest-dwellers who surpass me and who are my equals; there is no one in Sugrīva's company who is inferior to me.
t.5.37.39: Therefore enough of this anguish, O queen; let your grief depart. With a single leap those leaders of the monkey troops will come to Laṅkā.
t.5.37.38: If even I, such as I am, have reached this place, how much more could those mighty ones? For the foremost are not sent on errands; it is the lesser folk who are sent.
t.5.37.40: And those two great-souled lions among men, mounted on my back like the risen moon and sun, will come into your presence.
t.5.37.41: For those two heroes, the best of men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, united together, having come to the city of Laṅkā, will lay it waste with their arrows.
t.5.37.42: Having slain Rāvaṇa together with his hosts, Rāghava, the delight of the Raghus, will take you, O lady of beautiful hips, and return to his own city.
t.5.37.44: And when the lord of the Rākṣasas has been slain together with his sons, ministers and kinsmen, you will be united with Rāma, as Rohiṇī with the moon.
t.5.37.43: Therefore take heart, may good fortune be yours; be one who awaits the proper time. Before long you will see Rāma, blazing like the wind.
t.5.37.45: Swiftly, O queen, O Maithilī, you will reach the far shore of your grief, and before long you will see Rāvaṇa slain by Rāma.
t.5.37.46: Having thus consoled Vaidehī, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, resolved upon departing and spoke again to Vaidehī.
t.5.37.47: Soon you will see that Rāghava, slayer of foes and steadfast of soul, and Lakṣmaṇa, bow in hand, arrived at the gate of Laṅkā.
t.5.37.48: Soon you will see the heroic monkeys assembled together, whose weapons are their claws and fangs, who possess the valour of lions and tigers, and who resemble lordly elephants.
t.5.37.50: But Rāma, struck in his vitals by the dreadful arrow of Manmatha, finds no peace, like an elephant tormented by a lion.
t.5.37.49: O noble lady, you will see, on the slopes of Laṅkā and Malaya, troops upon troops of the foremost monkeys, resembling mountains and rain-clouds, roaring aloud.
t.5.37.51: Do not weep from grief, O queen; let nothing unpleasant touch your mind. For, like the devoted Śacī with Śakra, you have a protector in your husband.
t.5.37.52: Who else is there superior to Rāma, or anyone equal to Saumitri? Those two brothers, like fire and wind, are your refuge.
t.5.37.53: O Devī, you will not dwell long in this exceedingly dreadful place inhabited by hosts of rākṣasas. The coming of your beloved will not be long delayed; bear it only for the time it takes me to rejoin him.
